cur:manuscripts-escorial-rider-on-white-.summary: On a green ground, the haloed rider at the head of the column — the Word of God, Faithful and True — leads a file of riders on white horses, the armies of heaven, who carry swords. The repeated horses and riders create a powerful image of the final victory.
facts: The Escorial Beatus has 151 surviving leaves and 52 miniatures; it was probably made at San Millán de la Cogolla and was already in the Escorial library in the 16th century.
Its figures, with huge eyes and boldly patterned drapery, are among the most expressive in the Beatus tradition.
cur:manuscripts-escorial-rider-on-white-.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Among olive trees on a hillside, Christ, with a cross-nimbus and a red mantle, kneels in prayer toward the hand of God, while at the left the disciples sleep in a huddled group. The psalm is read as Christ's prayer in his agony before the Passion.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature. The exact psalm verse is not legible in the available image.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-12-christ.summary: From the upper left the Christ-Logos, holding a book, turns and directs the rays of a lighted torch onto the eyes of the bearded psalmist seated beneath a tree, answering his prayer, 'lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death'. An open sarcophagus lies at the psalmist's feet, and a group of enemies points at him in triumph. It is a vivid example of the illustrator turning a metaphor into an action.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-12-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-114-chris.summary: In a fiery pit at the left a personified Hades, clutching lost souls, stretches out an arm toward the young psalmist, who escapes him and supplicates the Christ-Logos, standing with three angels within a walled enclosure: 'the sorrows of death compassed me ... then called I upon the name of the Lord'. Children on the walls raise their hands to Christ — 'the Lord preserveth the simple'. The upper drawing of folio 67r is a compact image of deliverance from death.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-114-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

feat:santa-sabina-door-crucifixion.summary: A small panel on the great wooden doors of Santa Sabina shows Christ between the two thieves, all three with arms outstretched before a backdrop of buildings. It is often described as the earliest known publicly displayed image of the Crucifixion, made about a century after Constantine is said to have abolished crucifixion as a Roman punishment. Christ stands larger than the thieves with open eyes, alive and serene, his triumph over death already present in the moment of sacrifice.
facts: The doors are generally agreed to date from c. 430–432, when the church was being completed under the priest Peter of Illyria, though they may originally have been made for a larger doorway; they are among the oldest surviving carved wooden doors anywhere.
Of an original 28 panels, 18 survive, depicting scenes from the Old and New Testaments.
The crosses themselves are barely visible; the figures appear almost in the posture of prayer (orans), with only the nails in their hands indicating crucifixion.
The panel sits high on the door, so many visitors pass beneath it without noticing this landmark in Christian art.

feat:santa-maria-maggiore-adoration-of-t.summary: High on the triumphal arch of Rome's great basilica of the Virgin, the infant Christ sits alone on a wide, jewelled throne, attended by angels, while the Magi in Persian dress approach with their gifts. Rather than a baby in his mother's arms, he is shown as a small sovereign receiving homage, an image of the incarnate Word as King from the first moment of his earthly life. The arch's cycle of Christ's infancy is among the earliest surviving monumental sequences of its kind.
facts: The mosaics were made under Pope Sixtus III (432–440), whose dedication 'XYSTUS EPISCOPUS PLEBI DEI' ('Sixtus, bishop, to the people of God') still appears at the top of the arch.
The programme is closely linked to the Council of Ephesus (431), which proclaimed Mary 'Theotokos', the God-bearer, to defend the full divinity of the child she bore.
Mary appears beside the throne dressed like a Roman empress, and a second dignified female figure on the other side has been interpreted variously as a personification of the Church or a Sibyl.
The arch also includes rarely depicted episodes, such as the Holy Family's meeting with Aphrodisius, governor of an Egyptian city, drawn from apocryphal tradition.
